Dark matter was proposed because the gravitational behavior of very massive objects like galaxy clusters did not match their observable mass. Basically you add up everything you can see in a galaxy cluster and you have an idea how massive it should be. However, this observable stuff behaves gravitationally as if it were much more massive than we observe it to be, so there is "missing mass" that is unaccounted for. Dark matter is a proposed solution to this discrepancy. It would account for about 73% of the total mass of the universe and is thought to comprise the large-scale structure of the universe, around which all the observable matter collects.

Dark energy was a solution to a different problem. Gravity is a universal attractive force between matter. The universe began with a big bang that introduced a massive amount of energy that caused the universe to expand in opposition to gravity. If gravity and the energy of the big bang were the only forces at play, you would expect the expansion of the universe to gradually slow, then reverse as gravity took over, much like you when throw a ball up in the air, and it slows under the force of gravity, reverses direction, and returns to your hand. However, observations indicate that the expansion of the universe is actually accelerating, which would suggest there is another force at work acting in opposition to gravity. This is dark energy. It's not just leftover inertia from the big bang but a force that is actively pushing against gravity. Dark energy accounts for 23% of the mass of the universe, so if you add that to dark matter, 96% of the universe is composed of stuff we can't directly observe, leaving 4% for everything that we can obseeve, like stars, planets, people, and goats.

Well they have no charge, so how can they have an opposite charge? Well, neutron, and protons as well, are made of things called quarks, three of them to be specific, and they each have an individual charge, all stacking up to a net charge for the composite particle. The neutron is made up of two down quarks and one up quark, which have charges -1/3 and +2/3 respectively. That adds up to 0 net charge, while the protons quarks, two up and one down,for a net charge of 1.

The antiparticles of these two are made up of antiquarks, so the antineutron still retains it charge of 0. These particles, there are some more, made up of three quarks are called baryons, but there are also composite particles called mesons. Mesons are made out of two quarks. One "normal" quark and one antiquark bound together.

Some elementary particles, like the photon, are free of charge and not composite, therefore, they do not have an antiparticle.

The big thing about antimatter is that when it interacts with regular matter, koinomatter, it annihilates both the regular matter and the antimatter, and become pure energy. Why our Universe ended up being dominated by "regular" matter, instead of antimatter, is one of the big mysteries in modern physics, as the calculations predict an equal amount, which would just lead to constant annihilation and no planets or stars.

Now dark matter and dark energy is an whole other thing! And they actually don't really have anything to do with eachother, they are just called "dark" because we know so little about them.

Lets start with dark matter. Dark matter is the dominant form of matter in the Universe. It makes up 85% of all the matter, but it does not interact with anything but gravity. The only way we know it exist is because of how it warps spacetime. What we do know, more than that it exists, is that it is non-baryonic, that is, not made out of three quarks and... That's basically it!

Some people argue that it might be because of some things called MACHOs, massive astrophysical compact halo objects. That is dead stars, other stellar remnants and black holes. Searches for MACHOs and our models of the Universe says that can't explain all of the extra gravity though, and the leading theory today is something called WIMPs, weakly interacting massive particles.. Something we don't really know what it is either, more thant that it is massive, it has mass, and that it is weakly interacting, barely affected by anything but gravity, but it could be the particles predicted by the supersymmetry theories, which is a whole subject itself.

As you can see, we don't really know a whole lot about this stuff, so why are we so sure of it? Well, with it our current, otherwise working, models also work on grander scales and it is a whole lot smaller leap to dark matter, than that there would be something wrong in the model, especially since we can see different densities and distributions of dark matter, we know that there is "something" there at least!

Lastly dark energy.. Oh boy. This baby we know even less about. Dark energy is what drives the accelerated expansion of the Universe, and it is a huge amount. Dark energy makes up about 73% of all the energy in the Universe. (Remember E=mc^2, energy equals mass, so dark matter, and regular matter [also antimatter], is included in that percentage.) It exerts a negative pressure, not unlike the Casimir effect and is uniformally distributed in the Universe.

What is it, why does it exist? Well, there are three main theories, that are all plausible explanations. The first is the cosmological constant, and that basically just states that it is like it is, and there's no deeper explanation than that. The second one is that there is something outside our hubblesphere, out cosmological horizon, that is exerting a force, kind of like gravity, upon our whole Universe. Lastly is Heisenbergs uncertainty principle.

Heisenbergs uncertainty principle states: "We can't know the momentum and position of a particle exactly at the same time, only one of them". An equivalent way of stating this is that we can't know both the energy of a particle and the exact time the measurement was made, at the same time. We can know one, but not both, there will always be small uncertainty in at least one of them.

Now imagine an empty part of deep space. Lets say you have a box there and in that box you get rid of everything. Every little particle, every little bit of energy, just totally empty space. Then, within that box, you have 0 energy and you would know when you had 0 energy, but then you know the energy and time, and you would break the principle. This tells us that even empty space has an uncertainty. It is believed that in empty space, virtual particles pop in and out of existance and instantly annihilate eachother, within the time frame of that uncertainty principle. This gives rise to particles, and therefore energy, which drives the expansion, and since it is a property of vacuum, empty space itself, it will not be diluted as the Universe grows and expands.

I would like to add a deeper level of understanding to why anti-matter has the properties it does, and in turn exposes some of the great genius and audacity of the great scientist Paul Dirac. If one wants to expand regular quantum mechanics (which is innately assumed to be utilized for slow moving particles in much the same way that Newtonian physics is utilized for slow moving particles) to include relativistic effects (a theory which respects the fact that the speed of light $c$ is the universes's speed limit) one arrives (most generally, to exclude the Klein-Gordon equation) at the Dirac equation

$$ (i \hbar \slashed \partial -mc \mathbbm 1) \psi = 0 $$

where $ \slashed \partial $ which is the momentum operator now includes what is known as a particular "spin representation".

Solutions to this equation yeild not 1 but 2 (!) previously unknown / unconnected facts about particles.

  1. Antiparticles. General free particles solutions have the form of

$$ \psi ~ a^\dagger \exp{i E t / \hbar} + a \exp{-iE t / \hbar} $$

2x the normal solutions predicted by regular QM. Standard non-relativistic QM predicts the $a \exp{-iET} $ solution; so what do we do with the other solution which does NOT have the negative sign? This is a problem because we know that $i$ , $t$, $\hbar$ are all positive so the energy $E<0$ which is a huge issue because it means the ground state (the state with the smallest energy) is unbounded, or in essence on will fall down the energy well forever and never have a valid ground state (because one can always find a state with a smaller energy)

A second rate physicists would have just thrown out the first solution (much like throwing out a complex valued solution in classical mechanics) but Dirac decided to keep it. He proposed the philosophical idea of a "Dirac Sea" where for some reason, all of the negative energy states except 1 are unacceptable to the system (filled with other particles that do not interact, and nowadays we interpret this as a contribution to the vacuum). This is why anti-particles have opposite charge, if once considers the potential energy for a charge distribution

$$ V(r) = -k q / r $$

where $q$ is the charge $r$ is the magnitude of the distance from the charge and $k$ is some appropriate constant depending on what system of units you are using. The only way to make the electric potential energy negative (as is predicted by the pesky negative energy solution of the Dirac equation, is to make the charge opposite: hence for a negative energy state of an election (the famed positron anti-particle) the charge must be $+e$ as desired.
